lessons.title: ELSS Mutual Funds: Shortest Lock-In, Equity Returns

children.text: Every other option in Chapter 2 gave you a guaranteed or government-set return. ELSS gives you none of that. What it offers instead is the shortest lock-in of any 80C investment and the growth potential of the Indian stock market. For a young taxpayer on the old regime with a long horizon, that trade is often worth making. For someone who panics when the Nifty falls 15%, it can be a disaster. This lesson helps you figure out which one you are.

children.text: What an ELSS Fund Actually Is

An Equity Linked Savings Scheme is a diversified equity mutual fund with two special features: it must keep at least 80% of its money in stocks, and every unit you buy is locked for 3 years. In exchange, investments up to ₹1,50,000 a year qualify under Section 123 (80C) on the old regime. Most fund houses now name these funds with the words "ELSS Tax Saver", so they are easy to find on Zerodha Coin, Groww, Kuvera or directly on the AMC's website.

body.title: ELSS vs PPF: two very different ways to fill 80C

columns.label: ELSS
points: Market-linked: returns can be negative in any given year
No upper limit on investment (80C deduction capped at ₹1.5 lakh)
Long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year taxed at 12.5%
Regulated by SEBI, managed by a fund house
Suits long horizons and investors who can sit through market falls

columns.label: PPF
points: Government-set rate: 7.1% for July to September 2026
15-year tenure with partial withdrawals from year 7
Backed by the Government of India
Suits safety-first savers and the debt part of a portfolio

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: SEBI requires an ELSS fund to invest at least ___% of its assets in equity and equity-related instruments.
body.explanation: The 80% minimum is what makes ELSS an equity fund in substance. That is why its returns, and its risk, track the stock market.

children.text: The 3-year clock starts separately for each purchase. A lump sum is locked for 3 years from the day you invest. With a SIP, every monthly instalment has its own 3-year lock-in, so your SIP units unlock one month at a time.

body.caption: A ₹12,500 monthly ELSS SIP started in April 2026

body.title: Lock-In Check
body.question: Neel, a UX designer in Pune, invested ₹1,50,000 in ELSS: ₹50,000 as a lump sum on 15 June 2026 and ₹1,00,000 on 25 March 2027. On 1 July 2029 he needs money. How much of his ELSS can he redeem?
options: All of it, since the first investment is over 3 years old
Only the units from the ₹50,000 June 2026 investment
Nothing, since ELSS is locked for 3 years from the end of the tax year
Only the units from the March 2027 investment
body.explanation: Each purchase has its own 3-year lock-in from the date of allotment. The June 2026 units unlocked on 15 June 2029. The March 2027 units stay locked until 25 March 2030.

children.text: Returns: Higher on Average, Never Guaranteed

body.title: ELSS category average returns (CAGR) as of 13 August 2026

body.text: Look at the 1-year number. The same category that averaged about 13% a year over 5 years returned under 6% over the latest year, below PPF. In bad years, such as 2008 or early 2020, equity funds have fallen 30% or more in weeks. A 3-year lock-in is short enough that you can exit into a falling market. Treat ELSS money as money you will not need for at least 5 to 7 years, even though the law lets you out after 3.

children.text: Try it: a ₹12,500 monthly SIP for 3 years at an assumed 12% a year grows to about ₹5,43,846 on ₹4,50,000 invested. Now change the period to 10 or 15 years and watch how much of the final value comes from compounding rather than your own money.

Because of the lock-in, every ELSS redemption is held for more than 12 months, so gains are always long-term. Under Section 198 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (112A under the 1961 Act), long-term gains on equity funds are tax-free up to ₹1,25,000 in a tax year across all your equity shares and equity funds. Gains above that are taxed at 12.5%, plus cess. Unlike PPF, ELSS is not EEE: it is exempt on entry (old regime only), grows without yearly tax, and is taxed on exit above the threshold.

body.caption: The ₹1,25,000 exemption is shared across all listed equity shares, equity mutual funds and ELSS you sell in the same tax year.
₹1,50,000 lump sum in ELSS at an assumed 12% a year, no other equity gains in the year of sale

body.title: Your Turn: Tax on Redemption
body.prompt: Kiran, a civil engineer in Visakhapatnam, redeems old ELSS units in tax year 2026-27 with a long-term gain of ₹4,50,000. He has no other equity gains that year. What is his LTCG tax including 4% cess?
body.explanation: Taxable gain = ₹4,50,000 − ₹1,25,000 = ₹3,25,000. Tax = ₹3,25,000 × 12.5% = ₹40,625. Add 4% cess: ₹40,625 × 1.04 = ₹42,250. Had he spread the redemption over several years, using the ₹1,25,000 exemption each year, he could have paid far less.

body.text: Once units are out of lock-in, you can use the ₹1,25,000 yearly exemption deliberately: redeem enough units each year to book up to ₹1,25,000 of gains tax-free, then reinvest. This is called tax harvesting. Reinvesting in ELSS starts a fresh 3-year lock-in, so many investors reinvest in a regular flexi-cap or index fund instead.

cards.definition: Bought straight from the fund house or a direct platform like Zerodha Coin or Kuvera. No distributor commission, so a lower expense ratio and higher returns over time.
Bought through a distributor or bank relationship manager. The same portfolio as the direct plan, but a higher expense ratio to pay commission.
Gains stay invested and compound inside the fund. You pay tax only when you redeem. The default choice for most investors.
Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal: the fund pays out part of its value. Payouts are taxed at your slab rate, and reinvested payouts start a new 3-year lock-in.
The yearly fee charged by the fund as a percentage of your investment, deducted from the NAV. Check it on the fund's factsheet or on Value Research.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 provision that taxes long-term gains on listed equity and equity funds at 12.5% above ₹1,25,000 a year.

body.title: Scenario: FD or ELSS?
body.scenario: Siddharth, 34, is a chartered accountant in Mumbai on the old regime, in the 30% slab. After EPF and a term plan, his 80C gap is ₹1,00,000. He is saving for his son's college, about 12 years away. He already has an emergency fund. He is choosing between a 5-year bank tax saver FD at 6.50% and an ELSS fund. His plan is to invest the ₹1,00,000 as a lump sum in the last week of March, as he does every year.
body.prompt: Which option fits better, and what would you change about how he invests?
body.modelAnswer: ELSS fits his situation better. He has a 12-year horizon, an emergency fund in place and a professional understanding of risk. Both options give the same deduction: ₹1,00,000 × 31.2% = ₹31,200 in tax saved. The difference is what happens next. The FD's 6.50% (6.66% effective) shrinks to about 4.58% after tax at his slab, well below inflation over time. ELSS offers equity growth with gains taxed at only 12.5% above ₹1,25,000 a year, and only when he redeems. Two changes to how he invests: first, replace the March lump sum with a SIP of about ₹8,334 a month from April, which spreads his entry points across the market cycle and removes the year-end rush. Second, choose a direct growth plan to keep costs low, and do not redeem automatically after 3 years; the lock-in ending is not a reason to exit a 12-year goal. If he still wants some safety, splitting the gap between ELSS and PPF is a sensible middle path.

body.text: On the new regime, ELSS gives no deduction. AMFI asked for a separate ELSS deduction under the new regime ahead of Budget 2026, but it was not introduced. For new-regime taxpayers, a regular flexi-cap or index fund offers the same equity exposure and the same capital gains tax, without the 3-year lock-in.

body.title: Picking and Running an ELSS Investment
steps: Confirm you are on the old regime and have an 80C gap; otherwise consider a regular equity fund instead
Make sure you will not need this money for at least 5 to 7 years
Choose the direct plan, growth option
Compare expense ratios and long-term (5-year and 10-year) returns against the category, not just last year's top performer
Start a monthly SIP in April instead of a lump sum in March
Download the capital gains and investment statement from the AMC or CAMS/KFintech for your 80C proof
After lock-in, review whether to hold, harvest gains up to ₹1,25,000 a year, or switch

body.label: AMFI: Mutual Fund Data and NAVs
body.description: Look up any ELSS fund's latest NAV, scheme details and category data from the Association of Mutual Funds in India.

points: ELSS is an equity mutual fund with at least 80% in stocks and a 3-year lock-in, eligible under Section 123 (80C) on the old regime.
The lock-in applies separately to every lump sum and every SIP instalment.
Returns are market-linked: the category averaged about 12.93% over 5 years to August 2026, but under 6% over the latest year.
Gains are always long-term, taxed at 12.5% above ₹1,25,000 a year under Section 198 (112A).
Choose direct growth plans, invest through a SIP from April, and do not exit just because the lock-in ends.
On the new regime, ELSS has no tax edge; a regular equity fund gives the same exposure without the lock-in.
